title: How to Learn Buddhism
author: Zhiyu
excerpt: Learning Buddhism is itself spiritual practice — practice undertaken exactly as the Buddha taught.

inline.s: Learning Buddhism is itself spiritual practice — practice undertaken exactly as the Buddha taught.
This life’s goal: to end birth and death, and to deliver sentient beings.
In its cultivation there are steps by which one enters; in its realization there is a true attainment that one reaches on one’s own.
The Buddha said: “Though for a single lifetime one toils and labors, in but a brief moment thereafter one is born in the land of Immeasurable Life, with bliss without end.”

The aim of learning Buddhism is: to seek the Buddha’s Way above, and to transform sentient beings below. This is also the great mission of every student of the Dharma. How, then, is one to reach this aim and fulfill this mission?

To learn Buddhism, one must first arouse the bodhi mind, for the bodhi mind is the solemn vow of the great mission to attain Buddhahood and deliver sentient beings; it is the lighthouse for crossing the sea of birth-and-death suffering, and the driving force for braving the wind and waves.
Master Chewu said:
“If the great mind
(the bodhi mind)

is not aroused, then outwardly one cannot resonate with the Buddhas, and inwardly one cannot tally with one’s own nature; above, one cannot perfectly accomplish the Buddha Way; below, one cannot broadly benefit the multitudes of beings. How can one be released from love and attachment without beginning? How can one resolve grievances and enmities without beginning? The karmic offenses amassed over kalpas are hard to confess away; the wholesome roots amassed over kalpas are hard to bring to maturity. Whatever one practices, obstacles multiply; even should one achieve something, one ends by falling into the partial and the lesser. Therefore one must arouse the great bodhi mind in accordance with one’s nature.”
(The Posthumous Collection of Master Chewu)
Master Xing’an’s Exhortation to Arouse the Bodhi Mind says:

“The essential gate for entering the Way is to put the arousal of the mind first; the urgent task of practice is to give priority to establishing vows. Once the vow is established, sentient beings can be delivered; once the mind is aroused, the Buddha Way can be accomplished. If one does not arouse the vast mind and establish firm vows, then even after passing through numberless kalpas one still remains in the round of rebirth; though one may practice, it is all toil in vain. Hence the Flower Ornament Sūtra says: ‘To forget the bodhi mind and yet cultivate all wholesome dharmas is called the karma of Māra.’ If even forgetting it is so
(if forgetting the bodhi mind is already like this)
, how much worse never to have aroused it
(how much worse if one has not yet aroused the bodhi mind at all)
! Thus we know that whoever wishes to learn the vehicle of the Tathāgata must first fully arouse the vows of a bodhisattva; this cannot be delayed.”
Peng Jiqing’s Preface to Master Xing’an’s Posthumous Works says:

“In the past, when our World-Honored One had just attained perfect enlightenment, he exclaimed: ‘How wonderful! How wonderful! There is not a single sentient being who does not possess the wisdom of the Tathāgata. It is only because of deluded thought, inversion, and attachment that they cannot realize it. If they part from deluded thought, the all-knowing wisdom, the spontaneous wisdom, and the unobstructed wisdom will manifest before them.’ I have never understood
(I have long failed to understand)
this: why, for all the misery their deluded thought and attachment bring, do these sentient beings not part from them? And why, when it comes to the Tathāgata’s wisdom, do they still shrink
dàn
meaning “to shrink from difficulty”)
and not realize it? Yet in the end
zú
meaning “finally”)

they flee from their father, drift through long kalpas, and willingly become lowly hired servants, never thinking to turn back? There is no other reason: it is simply that they are not awakened. The bodhi mind is none other than a different name for awakening. The moment one awakens, the deluded thoughts and attachments before one are entirely the wisdom of the Tathāgata. For the Tathāgata’s wisdom has no essence of its own, taking the deluded thoughts of sentient beings as its essence; and the deluded thoughts of sentient beings have no essence of their own, taking the wisdom of the Tathāgata as their essence. Just as water forms waves, and every wave is water. From the very beginning, they are ultimately to abide in nirvāṇa without remainder. Therefore the difference between the awakened and the unawakened must never be concealed from oneself or befogged. Reflecting on this with sudden astonishment, and with a crack
xū
the sound of skin and bone separating)

, comprehension dawns; then the arousal of the bodhi mind will naturally be an overwhelming force that none can resist. Once this mind is aroused, the all-knowing wisdom, the spontaneous wisdom, and the unobstructed wisdom manifest before one — what need is there to seek anything elsewhere?”
The Venerable Xuyun said:
“Cultivation has no other cultivation; only recognize the head of the road. Once the road’s head is recognized, birth and death both cease.”
The Śūraṅgama Sūtra says:
“If the ground-cause is not true, the fruit will come out crooked.”

Therefore, for a student of Buddhism to possess right understanding is of the utmost importance. The curriculum of the Practice-as-Taught Online Buddhist Academy is designed so that, through systematic study and practice, one establishes right understanding and carries it out in one’s conduct.

Its course of study is divided into four stages: 1. ceasing evil and practicing good; 2. taking the precepts as the foundation; 3. prajñā dispelling delusion; 4. the Land of Ultimate Bliss as the refuge. The goals of cultivation are: to arouse the bodhi mind, to comprehend the ultimate truth, to have faith and vows and recitation of the name, and one mind undisturbed; to firmly grasp the fundamental theories of Buddhism, and to acquire the ability to read the original texts of sūtras and treatises directly, thereby laying a solid foundation for propagating the Dharma and benefiting beings. inline.s: Learning Buddhism is a process of turning evil into good, confusion into awakening, and the ordinary into the holy. Therefore the study of sūtras and treatises must ultimately be carried into actual practice (in thought and conduct).

The method of study and practice is: hearing → reflection → cultivation. Hearing is listening to the teaching (including reading it); reflection is pondering its meaning; cultivation is putting its meaning into actual practice. Through this process, we transform our ignorant views into right understanding and right views, and carry them into body (conduct), speech, and mind. In this process, repeated habituation is of the utmost importance; only through ceaseless habituation can one awaken into the Buddha’s understanding, give rise to the wisdom of discernment, and guide one’s own actions.
Generally speaking, when studying a sūtra or treatise, one should first divide it into a number of units, for instance by chapter or section.
First, for each unit:
Coarse reading. Read the unit three times to build an overall sense of it, so that you clearly know what the unit specifically contains.

Close reading. Divide it into paragraphs, write out the main idea of each paragraph and the central theme of the unit, and make sure every difficult character and difficult sentence is clearly understood.

Intensive reading. Through intensive reading, remember the meanings of technical terms, be able to recite the essential phrases and verses from memory, and be able to explain the unit — especially to expound on the difficult points and difficult sentences.
Then:
4. Master the whole book. The requirement is: write out the central theme and the overall thread of the whole book, and be able to summarize the entire book without looking at the text.

5. Habituation. Through ceaseless habituation, awaken into the Buddha’s understanding, give rise to the wisdom of discernment, and guide your own actions. This step is extremely important; one must constantly apply, test, transform, and elevate oneself amid circumstances.

For beginners, starting directly from the original texts of sūtras and treatises is quite difficult; it is best to begin from annotated editions. Once one has acquired a certain ability, one should read the original texts directly, for in this way the wisdom of discernment arises more readily. Therefore, when studying with annotated editions, one should deliberately cultivate the ability to read the originals directly. The textbooks of the Practice-as-Taught Online Buddhist Academy are designed precisely this way: they help one understand the sūtras and treatises being annotated, while also cultivating the ability to read other original texts directly. inline.s: Among the sentient beings of this Sahā world, the faculty of hearing is the sharpest. Listening while reading is often easier to understand and remember than reading alone. Therefore, while no textbook videos are yet available, one may use a text-to-speech tool to read the textbook aloud, listening as one reads. Moreover, one may also cultivate through repeated listening.

A text-to-speech tool is a tool that helps us study. Like any other tool, the more you use it, the more skilled you become, the more evident its effect, and the better you can apply it where it matters most. If you are not familiar with installing and configuring the software, ask a knowledgeable friend to help; you need only use it. (For the installation and setup of the text-to-speech tool, see
“Reading Web Pages Aloud by Computer”
The Lotus Sūtra says:

“The three realms have no peace; they are like a burning house. Filled with manifold sufferings, they are greatly to be feared. There are always the sorrows of birth, old age, sickness, and death — such fires blaze on without cease.”

Therefore, the Buddha taught the Dharma for forty-nine years, speaking of the sheep cart (the vehicle of the śrāvakas), the deer cart (the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas), the ox cart (the vehicle of the bodhisattvas), and even the great white ox cart (the Buddha vehicle), all in order to rescue sentient beings from this burning house of the three realms.

[Three realms] The desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm. The desire realm is the world inhabited by beings who still have the two desires of lust and food, extending from the six desire heavens above, through humans and animals in the middle, down to hungry ghosts and the hells below. The form realm is the world inhabited by beings who have ended the two desires of lust and food but still possess a form body, including the eighteen heavens of the four dhyānas. The formless realm is the world inhabited by beings who no longer have a form body but dwell with their mind-consciousness in profound and subtle meditative absorption, including the four formless heavens (the Heaven of Boundless Space, the Heaven of Boundless Consciousness, the Heaven of Nothing Whatsoever, and the Heaven of Neither Perception Nor Non-Perception). These three realms are all states in which ordinary beings undergo the round of birth and death; therefore the Buddhist practitioner first aims to end birth and death by leaving the three realms.

How, then, does one leave the three realms? The answer is: recite the Buddha’s name and seek rebirth in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss — this is the easiest, quickest, and surest path. And within the methods of Buddha-recitation, recitation of the name is in turn the easiest, quickest, and surest, praised by the ancient masters as “a shortcut within the shortcut (a shortcut among shortcuts).”

All other methods require one to cut off all afflictions in order to leave the three realms, whereas recitation of the name requires only that at the hour of death one’s recitation continue for ten recitations without interruption (unbroken by deluded thoughts), and one then resonates with Amitābha Buddha, is received and guided by him, and is reborn in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss (for details, see
“The Conditions for Rebirth”

). Compared with cutting off all afflictions, this is indeed vastly easier. And once one is reborn in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss, one’s lifespan is immeasurable; there are no manifold sufferings pressing in, but bliss without end; afflictions and karmic habits do not arise of themselves, and one immediately realizes the stage of non-retrogression. Under the guidance of Amitābha Buddha, Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva, and Mahasthamaprapta Bodhisattva, and with the mutual help and encouragement of the great assembly of pure bodhisattvas, one attains Buddhahood in a single lifetime and fulfills the great bodhi vows. Therefore recitation of the name is the most excellent method for ending birth and death. (For details, see
“Introduction to the Pure Land School”

[Resonance and response in the Way] The mutual communication between the response of sentient beings and the answering response of Amitābha Buddha. [Stage of non-retrogression] To advance only, never again to retrogress, until Buddhahood is attained.

There are many concrete methods of name-recitation, but their goal is all the same: to achieve ten uninterrupted recitations at the hour of death, to evoke the Buddha’s coming to welcome one, and to ensure rebirth in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss. As for how to recite the Buddha’s name, one may consult
“Awareness in Buddha-Recitation”
“Investigative Buddha-Recitation”
“The Essentials of Breath Buddha-Recitation”
, and other books and articles.

Question: Some groups and websites now name themselves after the “Pure Land school,”
such as the Chinese Pure Land School Association, the Primal Vow Temple of the Pure Land School, the Chinese Pure Land School
Global Pure Land School Portal, and so on
. What is going on?
Answer: All this is the mischief of Venerable Huijing of the Primal Vow school
(for this man’s background, see
“What Is the Primal Vow School?”

The term “Pure Land school” originally refers to the school among the ten schools of Buddhism that specializes in Buddha-recitation to seek rebirth in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss, taking Master Huiyuan of the Jin dynasty as its first patriarch,
a great school that has stood side by side with the Chan school for a thousand years and more

. Their so-called Primal Vow school, however, is nothing but a tiny sect; yet Venerable Huijing has gone so far as to name it the “Pure Land school,” as though they were the entire Pure Land school! This is a deliberate sowing of confusion, passing off fish eyes for pearls in order to deceive people who do not know the truth — especially beginners in Buddhism, who mistake them for the genuine Pure Land school and board their pirate ship. This is the very means by which the Primal Vow school lives:
deception!
Disciples of the Buddha must keep their eyes wide open;
whenever you encounter any group or website named after the “Pure Land school,” you must carefully discern whether it is the Primal Vow school, so as not to be taken in

. The method of discernment is simple: if it is led by Venerable Huijing, Venerable Jingzong, or others of that sort, and is trumpeting the views and theories of the Primal Vow school — for example the Chinese Pure Land School Association, the Primal Vow Temple of the Pure Land School, the Chinese Pure Land School
Global Pure Land School Portal, and so on — then it is the Buddhist-impersonating heretical Primal Vow school, and not the genuine Pure Land school;
their true names ought to be: the Chinese Primal Vow School Association, the Primal Vow Temple, the Chinese Primal Vow School
Global Portal, and so on — only then would name and reality match

[Ten schools] The Kośa school, the Satyasiddhi school, the Chan school, the Tiantai school, the Huayan school, the Shingon (True Word) school, the Dharma Characteristics (Yogācāra) school, the Pure Land school, the Vinaya school, and the Three Treatise (Mādhyamaka) school. Question: What does “beyond the three realms, outside the five elements” mean?

Answer: The “three realms” are the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm mentioned above. The “five elements” are a philosophical concept of ancient China, referring to the five great elements that constitute the material world: metal, wood, water, fire, and earth. “Beyond the three realms” means to transcend the round of birth and death; “outside the five elements” means to be free from the bondage and obstruction of the material world.
Question: Who is the Tathāgata?

Answer: “Tathāgata” is one of the ten honorific titles of the Buddha. Because the Buddha, riding upon the Way of True Suchness, came to attain perfect enlightenment and came into the three realms to teach and transform, he is called “Tathāgata.”
[The ten titles of the Buddha]

The Buddha has ten honorific titles: 1. Tathāgata — the Buddha, riding upon the Way of True Suchness, came to attain perfect enlightenment and came into the three realms to teach and transform; 2. Arhat (Worthy of Offerings) — the Buddha is worthy of the offerings of humans and devas; 3. Samyaksaṃbuddha (Perfectly and Fully Awakened) — the Buddha truly and fully knows all dharmas; 4. Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna (Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct) — the Buddha is fully endowed with the three kinds of knowledge (knowledge of past lives, the divine eye, and knowledge of the extinction of the outflows) and the five kinds of conduct (holy conduct, pure conduct, heavenly conduct, childlike conduct, and the conduct of illness); 5. Sugata (Well-Gone) — the Buddha, freely and well, goes and enters nirvāṇa; 6. Lokavid (Knower of the World) — the Buddha understands all the affairs and principles of the world; 7. Anuttara (Unsurpassed One) — the Buddha is the man of the highest and unsurpassed attainment; 8. Puruṣadamyasārathi (Tamer of Men) — the Buddha is the great man who tames and disciplines all sentient beings, leading them to leave defilement and enter nirvāṇa; 9. Śāstā Devamanuṣyāṇām (Teacher of Gods and Humans) — the Buddha is the teacher of all devas and humans; 10. Bhagavān (World-Honored One) — the Buddha is the one honored in common by all the world’s beings.
